title: Latency Tail Probing and Multi-Variant Scaling Retrospective
content:
Meeting: Architecture review / retrospective - Latency tail probing and multi-variant scaling
Date: 2024-10-14 10:00-11:30 PT
Venue: Eng retro room + Zoom
Attendees: Ava Chen (owner), Raj Patel, Sofia Martinez, Liam O'Connor, Maya Gupta, external perf consultant (recorded notes)
Goal: Review recent incidents where multi-variant rollouts caused unexpected p99+/p999 spikes, evaluate the probing approach used in canary/auto-scale decisions, and decide on a robust probing + scaling strategy for multi-variant serving.

1) Quick context and incident recap
- Incident summary: During a cross-tenant canary in eu-west, variant B (smaller quantized model) intermittently exhibited p99.9 spikes under synthetic conversational workloads. End-to-end request latency deadlines were missed for ~7 minutes, triggering failover to the fallback model.
- Observable signals: token-level latency saw bursts; per-variant KV-cache hit-rate dropped prior to spikes; CPU throttling on the host was not observed.
- Root-cause hypothesis: transient cold-paths for variant B combined with under-provisioned warm-up for KV-prefetch. Canary weight increased too quickly because our rollout controller relied solely on smoothed mean latency (p50) rather than tail metrics.

2) Design options discussed (high level)
A. Passive tail-aware rollouts: continue current rollout controller but add p95/p99/p999 gating thresholds; block weight increase if any tail threshold breached. Pros: low complexity; Cons: reactive, may cause slow rollouts for noisy workloads.
B. Active probing per variant: inject lightweight synthetic probes that exercise worst-case code-paths (long context, low cache hit) to estimate tail performance before raising weight. Pros: proactive surface of cold-paths; Cons: additional query load and complexity of probe placement.
C. Canary micro-burst testing: short-duration high-concurrency bursts against variant in a controlled slot to observe tail behavior at scale. Pros: realistic; Cons: risks transient production impact if not isolated.
D. Statistical risk model: combine probe results + historical tail distributions to compute a rollout risk score; use Bayesian update to decide weight changes. Pros: principled; Cons: needs data/infra work.

3) Benchmarking summary (what we ran this week)
- Micro-harness: we ran a 90s probe suite for three representative variants (baseline, quantized-8, int4-fused). Each probe exercised: long-generation (1k tokens), many short requests (concurrency 250), and conv-reentry (repeated reads to force KV eviction).
- Key results (median over 5 runs):
  - Baseline: p99=180ms, p999=430ms; KV-hit ~98%
  - Quantized-8: p99=220ms, p999=670ms; KV-hit ~92%
  - Int4-fused: p99=260ms, p999=1100ms; KV-hit ~88% and higher variance
- Observations: Int4-fused variant shows much heavier tail and larger variance under conv-reentry pattern; probes reliably reproduced the p999 spikes seen in the incident.

4) Safety / operational constraints considered
- Probes must not consume more than X% of a pool's headroom (proposal: 3%).
- Probes should be isolated to tenant-shared slots where possible (do not run probes on hot tenant exclusive slots).
- Probes must respect privacy: do not use real user data; use synthetic prompts and indoor corpora.
- Timebox probe execution and circuit-break if probe latency exceeds failure thresholds.

5) Decision (consensus)
- Adopt a hybrid approach: combine B (active probing) + D (statistical risk model) as the primary rollout safety mechanism.
  - Rationale: Probing surfaced the cold-paths that tail metrics alone missed; risk model allows rollouts to be data-driven and avoids overreacting to noisy single probes.
- Canary micro-burst testing (C) will be preserved as an escalation path for major model changes (architecture or quantization changes) where probes and historical data are insufficient.
- Passive tail gating (A) remains as a fallback safety net in the rollout controller.

6) Implementation plan (high level)
- Phase 1 (2 sprints): Probe harness + lightweight probe runners
  - Implement probe types: long-gen probe, conv-reentry probe, burst-concurrency probe.
  - Probe placement: runner runs in the same slot topology but attributed to a special system-caller so it can be throttled and isolated.
  - Metrics: collect p50/p95/p99/p999, KV-hit, memory working set, and probe success/failure rate.
  - SLO: probe overhead < 3% of pool capacity; probe execution time < 30s per probe.
- Phase 2 (3 sprints): Risk model and rollout controller integration
  - Simple Bayesian update model that ingests probe results + historical tail distributions; produces a risk score in [0,1].
  - Integrate with rollout controller to gate weight increases (> risk_threshold -> block). Default risk_threshold=0.2 (tunable).
- Phase 3 (ongoing): Observability and escalations
  - Add probe traces to runtime-console per-route view; expose probe risk score and historical distribution.
  - Define escalation: if probe risk > 0.6 escalate to SRE + perf on-call and enable micro-burst test.

7) Engineering tradeoffs and open questions
- Probe representativeness: how to ensure synthetic probes cover real tail triggers? (Action: collect anonymized signal profiles of user sessions that led to spikes; create probe templates.)
- Cost vs safety: probes add load; need to balance throughput commitments. (Action: quota/probe-budget feature in controller.)
- Probe frequency and scheduling: continuous, periodic, or on-demand during rollouts? (Decision: periodic + on-demand when variant introduced.)
- Failure modes of risk model: model needs to avoid being gamed by noisy probes; use ensemble of probe runs and fallback to passive gating.

8) Risks identified
- Over-conservative risk model could stall rollouts frequently, increasing manual review overhead.
- Under-provisioned probe runners could themselves cause noisy cache evictions.
- Edge cases: resource starvation windows (noisy neighbors) may still cause unpredictable tails not captured by isolated probes.

9) Action items (owner, due)
- Implement probe harness prototype (Ava Chen, 2024-10-28)
- Add probe metrics to metrics pipeline & dashboard (Sofia Martinez, 2024-11-04)
- Draft simple Bayesian risk model spec + evaluation plan (Raj Patel, 2024-10-25)
- Update rollout controller API to accept risk score and gating (Liam O'Connor, 2024-11-11)
- Create probe template corpus from anonymized incident traces (Maya Gupta, 2024-10-22)
- Schedule a dry-run: run probes + risk model on staging and compare outcomes with baseline rollouts (All, 2024-11-15)

10) Minutes / notes artifacts to keep
- Micro-harness benchmark outputs (S3 link placeholder: s3://redwood-perf/latency-probes/oct-2024/)
- Raw probe traces + flamegraphs (attached to PR #834)
- Risk model whiteboard sketch (confluence.redwood:/pages/risk-model-whiteboard)

11) Follow-up meeting
- Tentative date: 2024-10-28 09:30 PT (post-prototype demo)
- Agenda: demo probes, initial risk scores, integration blockers, updated gating thresholds.

Appendix: notes from discussion
- Maya: suggested adding a short lived "warmup burst" after variant assignment to reduce cold-paths; decided to evaluate as part of probe suite rather than primary mechanism.
- Raj: recommended conservative default thresholds for first-month rollout on multi-tenant pools.
- Liam: flagged rollout controller API surface changes that may touch infra contracts; requires sync with platform-engineering.
- Sofia: will prototype dashboards that show both probe-based risk and live tail metrics per-tenant and per-variant.

End of notes.
